#5028. Goldman Sachs More Than Doubles Its Bitcoin ETF Holdings to $1.28 Billion

Goldman Sachs more than doubled its spot bitcoin ETF holdings in the third quarter to about $1.28 billion, driven by a 52-fold jump in Fidelity’s fund, while cutting its stake in Strategy (MSTR) by more than half, a Monday filing shows.

The bank reported the positions in a Form 13F covering the quarter ended Sept. 30. Its long holdings across five spot bitcoin funds were valued at $1.283 billion, up from about $580 million in its filing for June 30, an increase of roughly 121%.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust remained Goldman’s largest bitcoin fund holding, at 16,440,599 shares worth $778.3 million. The share count actually slipped about 5% from 17,232,201 at midyear. The value rose because IBIT climbed from $33.29 to $47.34 a share during the quarter, a gain of about 42%.

The bigger change was in the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund. Goldman held 5,477,583 FBTC shares worth $397.9 million at Sept. 30, up from just 105,840 shares, worth $5.4 million, three months earlier.

Goldman also reported 2,000,020 shares of the Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust, worth $47.9 million. The fund, ticker MSBT, launched in April as the first bitcoin product from a U.S. bank-affiliated asset manager, with a 0.14% sponsor fee. Goldman’s June filing did not list it. The trust reported 36.42 million shares outstanding and $873.4 million in net assets at Sept. 30, so Goldman held about 5.5% of the fund.

The rest of the bitcoin fund book was smaller. Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust rose to 1,383,498 shares, worth $51.1 million, from 22,905. Goldman also listed 120,600 shares of the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust, worth $7.8 million, alongside puts on the same number of shares, which suggests that position is hedged.

The bank’s options book in IBIT is large, too. It reported puts on 7,513,000 IBIT shares, valued at $355.7 million, and calls on 4,895,600 shares, valued at $231.8 million. Those figures reflect the value of the underlying shares, not premiums paid, so they do not measure money at risk. Goldman runs one of Wall Street’s biggest market-making and derivatives businesses, and its 13F does not say which positions are hedges for clients and which are its own views.

The bank went the other way on Strategy. Goldman’s long position in the bitcoin treasury company fell to 2,760,766 shares, worth $422.6 million at Sept. 30, from 5,810,162 shares at midyear, a drop of about 52%.

Its Strategy put options barely moved, covering 4,738,700 shares worth $725.4 million, compared with 4,735,800 in June. Calls rose to 707,200 shares from 575,900. Strategy closed at $103.03 on Monday, down from $153.09 at the end of September, as the company keeps buying bitcoin and buying back preferred stock.

The pattern mirrors the one at Wells Fargo, whose own 13F, also filed Monday, showed its IBIT stake more than doubling while its Strategy position fell by about a third. JPMorgan reported $540 million in bitcoin ETFs in its third-quarter filing last week.

The Goldman positions are a snapshot as of Sept. 30, before bitcoin’s fall from above $83,000 to about $62,000 over the weekend. At Monday’s closing price of $36.79, the bank’s 16.4 million IBIT shares would be worth about $605 million, roughly $173 million less than the value in the filing.

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have been bleeding money since the quarter ended. IBIT lost about $2 billion over nine straight sessions through mid-November before taking in roughly $76.5 million on Monday.

The filing does not show whether Goldman added to or trimmed its bitcoin fund positions in October or November. That answer arrives with the fourth-quarter 13F, due in mid-February.

Wells Fargo’s long position in the bitcoin treasury company fell to 1,339,018 shares, worth $205.0 million at Sept. 30, from 1,994,253 shares at midyear, a drop of about 33%. Wells Fargo Securities also listed Strategy puts on 795,000 shares, down from 1.52 million. Strategy closed at $103.03 on Monday, against $153.09 at the end of September.

The filing lands as big banks disclose larger bitcoin exposure through ETFs and treasury stocks. JPMorgan reported $540 million in bitcoin ETFs in its own third-quarter 13F last week. Wells Fargo’s IBIT stake is more than four times that.

The timing also stands out. Since the quarter ended, U.S. spot bitcoin funds have been losing money fast. The fund took in about $76.5 million on Monday, breaking an 11-session streak of outflows that had pulled roughly $2.35 billion from IBIT since Oct. 30. That is almost exactly the value Wells Fargo put on its own stake at the end of September.

Wells Fargo’s filing is a snapshot as of Sept. 30. It does not show whether the bank or its clients bought or sold IBIT shares in October or November, the period in which bitcoin fell from above $83,000 to the low $60,000s. The next round of 13Fs, covering the fourth quarter, is due in February.

#5025. BlackRock holds 123,056 Strategy shares ahead of MSCI exit, but how much must it sell?

Three BlackRock ETFs reported 123,056 Strategy shares ahead of MSCI's Nov. 30 removal, raising questions about selling pressure.

When you buy an index fund, you're paying a manager to follow a particular group of stocks. MSCI creates these indexes and sets their membership rules, while companies such as BlackRock manage the funds that follow them.

MSCI is removing Strategy from several of its indexes after Nov. 30. Funds following those indexes will then be trying to match the performance of a group that no longer includes Michael Saylor's Bitcoin-buying company.

It's easy to see why investors expect selling: a fund that bought Strategy to follow an index loses that reason to own it when the stock drops out. But two BlackRock funds tracking the same MSCI index show why we can't simply add up all their investments and treat the total as a sell order.

One owns thousands of Strategy shares, while the other uses contracts with financial institutions to get the index's performance. Both managers have to account for the same change, but they don't have to do it through the same trades.

Their fund documents and published holdings let us follow part of that adjustment, including 123,056 Strategy shares reported by three BlackRock funds on Nov. 13, without pretending we know exactly how much stock will be sold at the end of the month.

MSCI's indexes put together stocks that meet a set of rules, such as company size and location, and assign each a share of the index's overall value.

A stock with a larger weight has more influence over how the index performs. The index serves as a benchmark, or performance target, for funds that follow it.

The MSCI USA Index includes large and midsize US companies, and Strategy's Class A shares are scheduled to leave it at the close of trading on Nov. 30, with the change taking effect Dec. 1. MSCI applied new eligibility rules for companies it classifies as non-operating, and Strategy was among the stocks selected for removal.

Other changes to specialized versions of MSCI's indexes are due to be announced on Nov. 18.

BlackRock's iShares MSCI USA ETF (MLRG) follows that US index and trades under the symbol MLRG. As an exchange-traded fund, investors buy and sell shares on a stock exchange while the manager handles the investments inside. Its published holdings included 5,227 Strategy shares on Nov. 13, worth about $583,000.

MLRG uses what's called representative sampling: the manager chooses a collection of investments designed to behave like the index without promising to own every stock on the list at every moment.

Its prospectus, the document setting out how the fund invests, says it intends to keep all or substantially all its assets in index stocks at roughly their index weights. It also allows some investments outside the index when they help the fund follow its performance, including around expected membership changes.

That gives the manager some flexibility while keeping the fund tied to its performance target. Strategy's departure is a reason to adjust the portfolio, but the documents don't require all 5,227 shares reported on Nov. 13 to be sold together at the Nov. 30 close.

BlackRock has another fund that follows the very same index: the iShares MSCI USA Swap UCITS ETF, traded in Europe under symbols including MUSD. This one owns a separate collection of developed-market stocks and uses contracts called total return swaps.

Under its investor document, the fund exchanges that stock portfolio's performance with financial institutions for the performance of the MSCI USA Index.

You're still buying a fund designed to follow MSCI USA, but the contracts provide that connection rather than a portfolio that reproduces the index stock for stock. When Strategy leaves, it stops contributing to the index performance those contracts are meant to deliver.

That doesn't tell us whether MUSD owns Strategy in its separate stock portfolio or whether it will sell any shares.

The counterparties of those contracts may also adjust their own investments to manage the risk they've taken on. Their trades aren't disclosed in these fund documents, so multiplying MUSD's assets by Strategy's index weight wouldn't tell us how many shares the fund has to sell.

BlackRock's iShares MSCI World ETF (URTH) follows companies across developed markets, including the US, and reported 29,345 Strategy shares, worth about $3.3 million, on Nov. 13.

Its iShares MSCI ACWI ETF follows companies in both developed and emerging markets and reported 88,484 shares, worth about $9.9 million, on the same date. These broader indexes include the US segment, so Strategy's removal from MSCI USA also affects them.

Together with MLRG, those funds held 123,056 Strategy shares valued at $13.74 million. We're looking at three identified portfolios on a particular day, rather than every fund affected by MSCI's decision.

Both URTH and ACWI also use representative sampling, so their managers have some flexibility in how they match their indexes.

Reported holdings on Nov. 13, 2026. This is a selected sample of iShares funds, not every MSCI-linked fund or a forecast of shares to be sold.

Source: iShares ACWI holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares URTH holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares MLRG holdings, Nov. 13, 2026

The iShares ESG Advanced MSCI USA ETF (USXF) follows a version of MSCI USA that applies additional screening rules to companies. It reported 16,144 Strategy shares on Nov. 13, but as of Nov. 17, the standard-index announcement doesn't establish what will happen in this particular version.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

MSCI's announcement for those specialized indexes is still due Nov. 18, so USXF isn't included in the three-fund subtotal.

Investors holding Strategy through a fund tied to another index don't automatically face the same change. For example, Invesco QQQ follows the Nasdaq-100, which has its own provider and membership rules.

Managers paid to choose stocks themselves can also keep assessing Strategy on their own terms, as can anyone who owns its shares directly.

Approximate Strategy holdings per $10,000 of fund assets on Nov. 13, 2026: reported portfolio weight divided by 100, then multiplied by $10,000. Inputs are rounded by iShares. These amounts are not forecasts of losses or required sales. USXF follows a screened index; its specific deletion treatment remains pending the Nov. 18 announcement as of Nov. 17.

Source: iShares USXF holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares MLRG holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares URTH holdings, Nov. 13, 2026 · iShares ACWI holdings, Nov. 13, 2026

In its response to MSCI's consultation, Strategy said that funds following the provider's global investable indexes held about 13 million of its shares, equivalent to 3.1% of basic shares outstanding.

That's a much broader estimate than the three-fund sample here, but the published statement doesn't identify the individual funds or give a current observation date for their holdings.

After the index changes, daily holdings files will let us compare what these funds owned before and afterward. Those files can show that a portfolio has fewer Strategy shares, but they won't necessarily show how the shares left it or why.

ETFs can grow or shrink as investors put money in or take it out. When a fund grows, its Strategy holding could increase simply because it needs more of the stocks it already owns.

Comparing the number of Strategy shares with the number of the fund's own shares helps separate fund growth from changes in how much of its portfolio it assigns to Strategy.

When an ETF shrinks, some stocks can leave through the process used to redeem its shares. Financial institutions can hand fund shares back to the ETF and receive underlying securities in return.

Strategy stock could leave the ETF without the fund itself selling it on an exchange, and the institution receiving that stock would then decide what to do with it. The next holdings file would record the smaller position without telling us about those later decisions.

MUSD adds another limit to what we can observe because its contracts deliver the index performance. Its counterparties could adjust their investments as Strategy leaves, but following only the fund's stock holdings wouldn't capture those decisions.

Even when we can see holdings change, comparing two dates won't show how much of Strategy's share-price movement was driven by MSCI, especially when investors can trade ahead of the announced change.

Strategy will still lose a place in the performance target these funds are paid to follow.

That could weaken demand for its stock and make raising money less attractive for a company that sells securities to finance Bitcoin purchases, although the index removal doesn't require Strategy to sell any Bitcoin itself.

#5021. The 40 Best Sci-Fi and Fantasy Books of 2026 So Far

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Featuring stories about app-based love, A.I., and way more. Sound familiar?

AS WE START to inch closer and closer to the end of the year, we know you’re going to be looking to feel cozy as the weather starts to get colder. Luckily, there are plenty of exciting sci-fi and fantasy books to curl up with a big mug of something hot with and read next to a fire.

There's new releases from mainstays like Jim Butcher and Matt Dinniman (two in fact, plus an upcoming TV show). There's all manner of space operas, cyberpunk thrillers, quests to kill gods, and even a wolf who sets out to kill the human race. And toward the end of the year, Emily St. John Mandel of Station Eleven fame returns with a new hopeful futuristic tale. As summer winds down, new books will continue to offer a much-needed escape throughout 2026.

Admittedly, there's been a lot of media begging for our attention this year, like The Odyssey, the World Cup, and soon Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three. But once the adrenaline of those action-packed watches wear off, it'll be the perfect time to crack open a new read and lock into assassins dealing with an alien invasion or a botched quest to clone the founding fathers (seriously).

Below is our list of the best reads of the year no matter what kind of sci-fi or fantasy you're interested in. Keep checking back as the year continues to progress for more updates.

A group of civilians are chosen to accompany veteran astronauts on a trip to Saturn's moon, Titan. They struggle to orbit the planet, and after some struggle, they manage to get back on course and return to Earth. But the Earth they left doesn't seem to be the planet they remember.

The 18th (yes, 18th!) book in Butcher's long-running Dresden Files series finds its titular character, Harry Dresden, struggling with grief. But Chicago is struggling, his brother is seriously ill, and he's now betrothed to a vampire. He'll have to put his own feelings aside to be the wizard everyone needs him to be.

Think dating is hard right now? Maybe you'll find solace in For Human Use, where a new app helps people find love with cadavers. You read that right. And as the app gains popularity, two men behind its funding and growth are pitted against one another.

Best known for his Dungeon Crawler Carl series, Matt Dinniman is back with a standalone novel. Oliver lives on the planet New Sonora, but when Earth decides to evict the planet's tenants, they make a deadly game of it, allowing Earth's gamers to use war machines for fun. Oliver decides to try and save his home no matter what.

Leena can see the dead, but keeps her secret closely guarded. When her brother falls ill, she decides to bargain away her secret to a dangerous merchant. Her trade leads her to a mysterious estate, where she has to fight for her life to escape the merchant's grasp.

The first in a new trilogy, Tao Wong's The First Step follows a young farmer who joins a school of cultivation, and begins a magical journey filled with martial arts, Chinese mythology, and a chance at immortality.

It's post-WWI Britain, and what people hope to be a time of peace is overtaken by a new threat. Fae are taking children, and one vet decides he'll be the one to bring them back.

If you don't normally read short story collections, now's your chance. Featuring award-winning and nominated stories, this book may be the perfect read to get you out of a reading slump with tales you can finish in one sitting.

A grief support group gets dark with the newest release from horror writer Eric LaRocca. After the death of his husband, Simeon becomes enmeshed with The Wretches, whose intense methods to process the death of loved ones leads Simeon to a mysterious man who promises they can all get one last moment with a loved one for a steep price.

The graduate of a deadly academy is the protagonist of Mark Lawrence's newest novel. Rue, now an old woman, is finally at peace with her violent upbringing. But as soon as she thinks she's entered retirement, the sins of her past come back to haunt her.

Trees can drag you to your death. Artificial monsters stalk the lands. And alien men wander around town. John Maraintha is dropped on the planet Scythia and has to find a way to adapt and survive.

Fans of classic folktale retellings will enjoy this take on The Little Mermaid. Rather than following Ariel, it centers on her granddaughter, who is awash in complex politics after the assassination of her father. To save her family's legacy, she makes a deal with the famed sea-witch Ursla.

If you're a fan of The Substance, you may enjoy this new book. A young struggling writer named Maggie meets an established producer who's looking to revive her career. The solution to both of their problems is an experimental procedure–that takes Maggie's youth and gives it to the older producer–along with a $3 million payout that helps with Maggie's money troubles. But both women quickly realize that the blood transfusion is anything but a simple transaction.

Space operas are a sci-fi subgenre that never get old. When a starship's crew returns to their home galaxy after a decade away, they find the once peaceful space they knew is now on the brink of war–and they're expected to fight in it. It's up to the ship's captain to make life or death decisions that may have irrevocable impacts on her crew.

A ten-year-old girl goes on a journey with her AI toy to reach New York in this novel all about the complex relationship between man and machine.

This debut follows a billionaire who has prepared for the apocalypse and is ready to survive in his bunker with his family. But above ground, raiders are also fighting to stay alive, and aren't too happy with their new neighbors.

Earth is in ruins. A colony ship on the way to its new home keeps its original civilians in cryostasis, while their descendants maintain the vessel on its four hundred yearlong journey to a new planet. But midway through the trip, the crew of descendants starts to wonder why they're spending their lives in service of a world they'll never see.

A beloved actor in an epic fantasy franchise where much of the characters believe the world is real makes a bold choice to break out of the false reality the studio has built, and convince his co-stars to go with him.

The eighth, highly anticipated book in the Dungeon Crawler Carl series picks up on the tenth floor, where Carl and Donut try to make sense of the system AI's mysterious plans and learn more about why it calls the eleventh floor 'A Parade of Horribles'.

If you're yearning for an epic tale of political intrigue, this new Ann Leckie read is for you. The empire of Radch is dealing with internal turmoil, and when a major decision is made on the religious site called Radiant Star, that turmoil could result in irrevocable changes to everyone in the city of Ooioiaa.

#5020. Trezor Shipping Partner Breach Exposes 27,000 Orders as Customers Report Scam Calls

Trezor said Monday that a data breach at Skladon, one of its shipping partners, exposed personal information tied to about 27,000 hardware-wallet orders, and that some customers have already reported scam calls. The company’s own systems were not compromised, and no wallet backups, PINs or passphrases were involved.

Skladon notified Trezor on Nov. 15 of unauthorized access to systems that held customer shipping data. The breach itself took place on Nov. 7. Trezor believes the attacker exported records for orders placed between Aug. 9 and Nov. 7. An investigation is ongoing.

The exposed records included full names, phone numbers, delivery addresses, email addresses, order dates, and the products purchased and their prices. Trezor said neither it nor Skladon ever holds wallet backups, PINs or passphrases, so the breach does not, by itself, let an attacker move a buyer’s bitcoin. It does give a stranger a home address and proof that the person bought a device designed to store crypto.

Anyone who received Trezor’s incident email and ordered in that window was affected. A small number of customers who ordered between Aug. 9 and 14 may also be included, but the company cannot email them because those details had already been anonymized under its 90-day retention policy. It is reaching those buyers through its blog and posted the same warning on X. Skladon does not ship to the United States, Trezor said, so U.S. customers were not affected by this incident. The company added that Skladon delivers to many countries, and that the leak is not limited to one region.

Trezor told customers to treat any unexpected call, text, email or letter about their order as suspicious, and to be alert to potential risks to their physical security. Scammers may quote real order details, including what was bought and what was paid, to make a message look genuine. Some customers have already reported scam calls.

“Trezor will never cold-call you or ask for your wallet backup,” the company said. Customers should contact support only through the company’s website, never through a link, QR code or number in an unsolicited message, and should never enter a wallet backup anywhere except on their device. If a message contains a threat or makes someone feel unsafe, Trezor said to contact local police first.

This is not the first time a Trezor contractor has lost customer data. In August, a breach at shipping provider ShipMonk exposed records from 13,689 customers, including 11,742 with full names, emails, phone numbers and shipping addresses. Trezor later said another approximately 67,000 U.S. customers who ordered between November 2019 and August 2021 were also affected, after ShipMonk failed to delete records it had assured the company were gone.

In September, a breach at marketing platform Brevo let an attacker send a phishing email through Trezor’s account and, the company later confirmed, export 347,149 newsletter addresses. Trezor took down the malicious domain within 20 minutes, but about 2,500 people had already clicked the link.

“We know this is not the first time customer contact details and addresses have been exposed in an incident involving one of our partners,” Trezor said Monday, adding that it is sorry, especially to anyone affected again. Hardware-wallet makers have faced this risk before. In 2020, an unauthorized party accessed Ledger’s e-commerce and marketing database, leaking over 1 million email addresses; Bitcoin Magazine later reported that more than 200,000 people also had home addresses exposed, and that some victims were later mailed fake devices.

In response, Trezor said anonymous pickup is now available in 18 European countries, so a name and home address need not reach the company, and that it is working to launch the option in the United States. It is also cutting how long it keeps order data from 90 days to 45, with plans to reduce that period further, and it has informed the data protection authority. The company said it is reviewing its relationships with third-party partners and the security requirements it places on them.

#5018. Three wallets hoard $52.7M on XRP’s sidechain, and nobody is trading it

Three addresses control nearly $53 million in USDf on XRPL EVM, raising questions about liquidity concentration and XRP demand.

Three addresses hold virtually all the dollar-pegged USDf token supply on XRP Ledger (XRPL) EVM, an XRP-powered smart contract sidechain, according to a Nov. 17 explorer snapshot.

The contract contains 52.9 million tokens, while DefiLlama values the chain's tracked bridged stablecoin inventory at about $52.7 million.

DefiLlama reports $22,415 in total value locked (TLV) in tracked DeFi protocols and just $0.09 in chain fees over 24 hours. Tokens are present, but measured application activity and fee expenditure remain small.

XRPL EVM is a separate blockchain from the native XRP Ledger. Its official documentation describes a sovereign layer-1 that runs Ethereum-compatible smart contracts and uses XRP for transaction fees.

That gives XRP a direct role in operating the chain, without making every dollar bridged there a dollar spent buying XRP.

On Nov. 17, the USDf contract metadata showed a supply of 52,906,708 tokens. The holder list showed four balances: 40 million USDf in the largest, about 7 million in the second, and 5.9 million in the third.

Those positions represent about 75.6%, 13.25%, and 11.15% of supply, respectively. The fourth address, labeled SquidMulticall, held one smallest unit, or 0.000000000000000001 USDf.

The three large addresses have no names or public tags in that response, so they cannot safely be described as three independent investors, customers, or beneficial owners.

A November 17 snapshot on XRPL EVM shows virtually all indexed USDf supply concentrated in three addresses, plus dust in a fourth.

The largest address holds about three-quarters of USDf supply; concentration alone establishes neither ownership nor economic use.

DefiLlama's Nov. 17 stablecoin API entry records 52,906,708 circulating dollar-pegged units and a dollar valuation of $52,674,373.43, implying about $0.9956 per unit.

The $22,415 DeFi total measures another category. Under DefiLlama's methodology, chain TVL sums assets deposited in tracked protocols, while bridge TVL is excluded from chain totals. The difference between inventory and TVL cannot be read as missing money, or used to establish that every token outside tracked protocols is idle.

Tokens can be present without the data demonstrating deep trading liquidity, broad participation, or sustained borrowing and lending. Dollar TVL also changes with token prices, making token balances and application activity necessary companions to the valuation.

The same DefiLlama dashboard reported zero in tracked decentralized-exchange volume over 24 hours and $5.37 over seven days, with its reported chain fees at $0.09 over 24 hours.

The chain explorer series counted 1,365 on Nov. 16, the latest full calendar day, following 1,004 on Nov. 15 and 1,020 on Nov. 14.

Paying fees uses XRP, but the stock of USDf does not establish fresh XRP purchases, the size of users' XRP holdings, or persistent demand to replenish them.

Broader balance distribution, usable trading depth, and repeated application transactions would strengthen the case for functioning liquidity.

Repeated XRP fee expenditure would demonstrate continued gas use, while evidence of fresh purchases would be needed to establish new buying demand.

#5017. The Next Generation of Weight-Loss Drugs Is Reshaping People’s Looks—And Not in a Flattering Way

WHEN YOU LOSE weight through traditional diet and exercise, you tend to see a gradual slimming down of your face. But when you add in gray-market peptides like retatrutide, you’re expediting the weight loss process. That also includes rapid fat loss in the face, leaving a sunken and hollowed-out look people are dubbing “reta face.”

Online Reddit communities on peptides and biohacking are packed with people commenting on changes to their facial appearance after taking retatrutide—a triple hormone agonist of the GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors that’s expected to become the next generation of weight-loss injections. One clinical trial found those taking retatrutide had more than double the weight loss of people taking Ozempic.

To be fair, “Ozempic face” has also been an issue. But with Eli Lilly expected to apply for FDA approval of retatrutide in early 2027 for obesity and other conditions, doctors say reta will likely cause more facial volume issues. Is there any way to prevent these unflattering side effects? We went straight to the doctors currently treating people with facial symptoms from GLPs.

WHILE RETA FACE isn’t an official medical diagnosis, it’s a real phenomenon. “The facial changes can be kind of dramatic,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. But the lack of criteria has also caused some debate over what qualifies as reta face.

On the r/BodyHackGuide community (with over 87,000 contributors dubbed “Lab Rats”), reta face before-and-after posts are recurring discussion threads. Some describe reta face as a chiseled look after weight loss while Ozempic face is the more sickly face. Others argue that “reta face” and “Ozempic face” are simply two terms to describe the sunken look from your face losing fat.

“Reta face is the new Ozempic face,” says dermatologist Gary Goldenberg, MD. “Since retatrutide is a triple biologic agonist that produces more significant weight loss than GLP peptides, patients may have an even more exaggerated appearance of a sunken, aged look.”

That means cheeks can become flat and hollow, temples narrow, and undereye areas can look sunken and dark. “Facial bones can also become more prominent as fat disappears,” says Dr. Goldenberg. “The skin can thin, as collagen and elastic fibers have less underlying fat plumping them up.”

Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research in dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital, says the shape of your face changes with any significant weight loss—it’s just more apparent when someone is on a weight-loss medication.

ABSOLUTELY. DR. ZEICHNER says minimizing the appearance of facial wasting is all about losing weight slowly—even when taking a GLP-1 or reta. While you can’t target specific areas for fat loss, Dr. Goldenberg recommends pacing yourself while still getting plenty of protein on your plate and being selective about meals that have enough nutrients.

If you already have reta face and the appearance bothers you, Dr. Goldenberg recommends seeing a dermatologist. “Collagen stimulators and fillers are a very common treatment for this problem,” he says. “Volume can be restored and contouring can be improved with these treatments.”

#5015. Coinbase Launches ChatGPT Plugin for Trading Bitcoin, Stocks, and Derivatives

Coinbase launched an official plugin for ChatGPT on Tuesday that lets users connect a Coinbase account and trade bitcoin, other cryptocurrencies, stocks and derivatives without leaving the conversation, provided they approve every order.

The company said the tool puts trading “in the same chat you use for everything else.” Users can connect an account, review a portfolio and place orders from ChatGPT on the web, on mobile or on desktop. Chief executive Brian Armstrong wrote that “starting today anyone with ChatGPT can connect their Coinbase account” and can “trade right inside your Coinbase account.”

Coinbase posted a link to the official plugin in ChatGPT’s directory. Its developer documentation describes a short setup: sign in, review the access being requested and choose which portfolios the plugin can see. Interactive confirmation cards in the chat cover new orders, edits, cancellations and conversions between dollars and USDC. Read-only requests, such as checking a balance, do not use them.

The announcement did not single out bitcoin, but the plugin sits on the same rails as Coinbase for Agents, the company’s toolkit for connecting AI apps to a trading account. That documentation lists spot trading in more than 900 pairs, including bitcoin, along with eligible U.S. stocks and dated futures from Coinbase Financial Markets. The examples include a market buy of bitcoin and a dated bitcoin futures contract. Orders go through Advanced Trade, so those fees and eligibility rules apply. Fees vary by product, fee tier and whether an order adds or takes liquidity, and they are shown on the order preview.

The official plugin is narrower than the full agent toolkit. A separate custom connection is required for the company’s Global Derivatives products and for x402 payments, which agents can use to buy market data. Coinbase already offers U.S. customers stock and ETF trading on its own platform, but the agent documentation says equity orders trade during regular market hours by default. The plugin should not be read as a new around-the-clock stock venue. What a user can buy still depends on the products already attached to that account.

Armstrong’s “anyone with ChatGPT” line is broader than the documentation. The official plugin is currently available to U.S. Coinbase users, and availability also depends on a user’s ChatGPT account and workspace. If the plugin does not appear, the company tells users to check their workspace’s plugin policy. In a disclaimer attached to Tuesday’s announcement, it said product availability, eligibility and Coinbase entities “vary by jurisdiction,” that trading can result in a total loss, and that “AI agents may fail.”

The same post said users direct all AI activity and assume full responsibility. The developer documentation adds that agents can misinterpret instructions or produce inaccurate output, and that the user is responsible for reviewing and authorizing trades. Access can be revoked later in an account’s security settings, under connections.

OpenAI’s help pages describe a distinct Finances feature in the United States that can connect bank and credit-report data but cannot place trades, and note that third-party plugins that support transactions are a separate product.

Tuesday’s plugin is the most visible version of work the company has been shipping for months. In June, it introduced Coinbase for Agents, a login and a command-line tool that let an AI app trade inside limits set by the user, including a gradual rebalancing toward a bitcoin-heavy portfolio. On Nov. 11, it added Agent Controls, server-side caps on trade size and 24-hour volume, plus an auto-stop if a portfolio falls by a set percentage. Those controls live on the company’s servers, so an agent cannot switch them off.

The official plugin is meant for people who want to stay in the loop. The company also documents a custom ChatGPT connection for automated workflows that does not add a confirmation card before each trade, though sign-in, consent and authorization for financial actions still apply. For the official plugin, every bitcoin, stock or derivatives order still needs a human yes.

Cleaner, healthier teeth with picks for every budget and style of brushing.

YOU ALREADY KNOW you need to brush at least twice a day, no matter what toothpaste or mouthwash you use. But technique matters just as much. Even for me—a grooming editor who writes about this stuff—it can feel like a chore. In the morning, I brush before coffee when I’m barely awake. At night, I’m wiped out from the day or drifting off for less wholesome reasons. That’s why I love electric toothbrushes: they simplify brushing and deliver a better clean by doing most of the work for you.

Unlike manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrushes use vibrations and automated head movement to remove plaque and debris. Many models include smart programs for whitening or gum care, interchangeable heads for sensitive or deep cleaning, and built-in timers. Some of the latest options even feature AI that tracks your brushing and suggests improvements.

But the main selling point of electric toothbrushes is their ability to clean more thoroughly and efficiently than manual options, using power and vibrations no hand can match. Top-tier electric toothbrushes can be pricey, but they’re an investment in your smile. It’s the closest you can get to a dentist-level clean at home.

For the past two years, the Oral-B Series 10 has been listed at the top of this list. It remains the best overall electric toothbrush; however, it’s currently sold out everywhere due to this demand. The model that immediately preceded it, the iO Series 9, is the next best thing. It features many of the same features and power, just with a less high-tech charging mount (which may be a benefit for some who prefer something lighter and less complicated).

Series 9 is similarly a premium electric toothbrush packed with advanced features designed to elevate your oral care routine. Just like the 10, there are seven customizable modes—including Daily Clean, Sensitive, Super Sensitive, Intense, Gum Care, Tongue Clean, and Whitening—this brush adapts to your needs, whether you have sensitive gums or want a deep clean. Its oscillating, vibrating round brush head provides a powerful yet gentle clean, and the built-in pressure sensor ensures you're brushing with the right amount of force, lighting up red (too strong), blue (too weak), or green (just right) based on your pressure.

The Series 9 pairs with a companion app to track your brushing in real time across 16 zones of the mouth, offering instant feedback and a visual map of missed areas. I’m not a huge tech junkie, especially when it comes to something like brushing my teeth, since I just want to get it over with quickly. But this is one of the few apps that genuinely adds value, with accurate tracking, clear visuals, and brushing reminders.

Even if you skip the app, the built-in display shows your selected mode and a timer, though the latter is easier to read in the app. That being said, it’s nearly impossible to achieve a 100 percent clean according to the app (I usually aim for between 80 and 90) without brushing for five or more minutes, which is not recommended because it can damage enamel. If you’re a perfectionist, this will prove annoying.

In terms of design, the Series 9 is sleek and solid, and comes with a sturdy travel case. It charges in just three hours (significantly faster than most others on this list) and comes with four replacement heads, which should cover your first year of use if you replace them every three months, as dentists advise.

If you prefer sonic, this toothbrush offers nearly the same level of features and effectiveness as the Oral-B iO Series 9. At $340, it's also one of the most expensive electric toothbrushes, but the price includes five modes and three intensity settings to fully customize your brushing experience, along with an innovative charging cup.

Interchangeable brush heads, specifically designed for tasks like whitening or tongue cleaning, also help you achieve optimal results with minimal effort. Similar to the Series 9, it also has app-enabled smart modes that provide personalized feedback on your brushing habits and overall progress. Plus, the charging travel case makes it easy to travel while protecting your investment.

Women’s Health Associate Style and Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz has been using this toothbrush for the past year and says it’s the cleanest her teeth have ever felt. “I’ve long been using an electric toothbrush, so I didn’t expect to be too blown away by this one. I was wrong.” She likes how it pairs multiple brush heads, cleaning modes, and a timer with real-time app feedback to keep her brushing technique on track. The sleek charging cup also makes storage and charging effortless, even on a tiny sink, she says.

Read More: Are Electric Toothbrushes Better?

Men’s Health Associate Producer Janie Booth says the round, oscillating head reminds her of the tool dental hygienists use to polish teeth during a professional cleaning. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both of which are easy to pack. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long.

Booth says she’s used it for a month without recharging once. If your biggest concern is avoiding charging as much as possible, the Rev is your best bet. The battery even outperforms the Oral-B iO Series 9 and Philips Sonicare DiamondClean, both of which are roughly $300 more expensive.

I’ve used all three as my daily driver at different times, and the Rev battery lasts at least a week longer. You can expect to get at least 5 weeks from a single full charge with twice-a-day use. The rest of its offerings are pretty minimal, though, again, this will be welcomed by newcomers. It only offers three levels of intensity, but none are too strong for sensitive teeth.

However, they’re not quite as powerful as the most intense settings on Oral-B and Philips, though they are close. The Oral-B iO Series 9 offers about 10,500 oscillations per minute on its Daily Clean setting, while the Rev goes up to 9,630 oscillations per minute. Considering the $300 price difference between the two, the slight dip is a worthy trade-off.

Before I upgraded to an electric, I was a devotee of Colgate’s Active Prevention Foaming Toothbrush. The heads are as soft as they come, and the handle fits perfectly in my hand. Naturally, I was thrilled when the brand made an electric version, adding vibration to those two core features. To be clear, this is battery-powered, so it’s not rechargeable. But you also don’t need to worry about recharging it every couple of weeks. I get a little more than a month out of each set of batteries (two AAAs), so while it’s under $15 at first, I plan to spend more over time.

Still, I haven’t tried a battery-powered toothbrush that lasts that long without sputtering or losing efficiency, like Colgate’s can. It’s not the most powerful electric toothbrush, as Colgate doesn’t even list its vibrations per minute (which usually means it’s nothing to write home about). But I’ve yet to find a battery-powered toothbrush that can compete with the power of rechargeable options, so it’s inherent to the design.

No matter your background, everyone shares one truth: we all lie to our dentists about flossing. They see through it, and they roll their eyes for good reason. Daily flossing is essential, which is why Waterpik built a toothbrush with an integrated water flosser. Its all-in-one design lets you brush and floss at the same time, saving effort while leaving your teeth feeling dentist-clean.

The brush includes two intensity modes and a timer, but the standout is the built-in Waterpik. You can brush with or without the water flosser, though why skip it? While it doesn’t offer the smart features of higher-end models, the unique water flosser justifies its higher price tag. Plus, its 30,000 vibrations per minute match those of the similarly priced Zina45. In that sense, it’s like the water flosser is free.

This toothbrush offers 33,000 vibrations per minute, four custom settings, a two-minute timer, and soft, nylon bristles. It’s everything you need for a decent electric toothbrush. However, there are two features that help it stand out. For one, the magnetic USB touch charger is super convenient, making recharging as simple as any option on this list. As someone who regularly forgets to recharge his devices, I appreciate how easy this one makes the process.

It also comes with a polishing head, one of the few electric toothbrushes that do. This tiny rubber head is designed to make your teeth look smoother and shinier by focusing on surface stains and plaque removal rather than deep cleaning between teeth. I use mine after brushing, even if I brush with a separate toothbrush, to complete the full at-home dentist-level clean. It also comes with four replaceable polishing heads, so you won’t have to worry about replacing them for some time.

At first, the smaller toothbrush head on the Suri 2.0 felt less effective than the OG model, but over time, it delivers the same clean. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both designed for travel. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long. It’s the only other electric toothbrush we’ve tested that lasts over a month on a single charge, though I find it’s a couple of days shorter than the Quip Rev.

This brush delivers 33,000 vibrations per minute yet remains whisper-quiet. Its sleek case hides a UV-C light that kills 99 percent of germs on the brush head, keeping it clean wherever you take it. Plus, the head and bristles are eco-friendly, made from recyclable, plant-based cornstarch and castor oil. Overall, it’s powerful, sustainable, and travel-ready.

When choosing an electric toothbrush, you’ll need to decide between a sonic or oscillating brush head. There isn’t one right answer; it just comes down to preference.

Toothbrushes have gone smart, too. Most models include the basics—a strong motor and a built-in timer—but many now add extras like brushing modes, pressure sensors, and even AI to track your habits and coach you to improve. The right features depend on what matters most to you.

Brushing your teeth is personal, shaped by your own needs and quirks. To find the best electric toothbrushes for every sensitivity and style, we tapped a wide group of Men’s Health testers. I spoke with dentists about their go-to brands, pulled in feedback from our original 2019 guide, and compiled a list of top contenders. I then distributed these toothbrushes to writers and editors, each of whom tested them for at least a month to judge comfort, ease of use, and long-term effectiveness. Based on that feedback, here are the eight best electric toothbrushes for men in 2026.

As with manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrush heads need to be replaced every few months. Because the latter tend to be more expensive, this makes owning electric models more expensive. I recommend buying the heads in bulk when available, as this can make for pretty substantial savings. Electric toothbrushes have more nooks and crevices than their manual counterparts, which means they require a little extra daily maintenance.

This means carefully rinsing them after every use to stave off funky toothpaste and spit residue. It’s also worth actually removing the brush head from time to time to wipe the attachment point where the head meets the handle. A cotton swab or even your old toothbrush is usually enough to do the trick.

It’s tempting to just toss old toothbrushes and toothbrush heads in the trash once they’ve outlived their usefulness. But they’re actually perfect for detailed cleaning work that requires moderately stiff bristles to clean out tight spaces. Think: Shower heads, hiking boots, bathroom grout, your dishwasher filter, bird feeders—you get the idea.

#5013. Bitcoin faces a liquidity drain as Anthropic IPO unlocks millions

Anthropic’s IPO unlocks test Arthur Hayes’s $1.245 trillion AI selling scenario and its potential impact on Bitcoin liquidity.

Anthropic’s planned IPO brings a real risk of insider selling, but its share-release schedule does not make a drain on Bitcoin liquidity inevitable.

Arthur Hayes’s Nov. 5 essay puts falling AI share prices at the start of a broader credit squeeze. He argues that insider sales will weaken stocks, make borrowing more expensive or unavailable, curb bank-balance-sheet growth, and reduce the dollar liquidity supporting crypto.

Hayes estimated 83% dilution by June 2027, arguing that roughly $1.245 trillion in new capital would be needed to absorb potential selling at a hypothetical $1.5 trillion IPO valuation.

Anthropic provides a concrete test of the first link, since its offering creates new shares, while subsequent releases also permit existing holders to sell.

Those changes affect supply differently, with different consequences for company fundraising and investors’ ownership.

Anthropic’s Nov. 10 announcement proposes 825 million Class A shares, with 801,351,354 offered by the company and 23,648,646 by existing stockholders, and the AI firm receives no proceeds from the existing holders’ sales.

The preliminary price range is $70 to $78, with an option for underwriters to purchase another 123.75 million shares.

New company shares increase the outstanding share count and raise money for Anthropic. Secondary shares already exist, and selling them transfers ownership and pays the selling holder. A later unlock removes a restriction on selling without issuing another share.

Anthropic proposes new company shares alongside existing-holder shares. Follow each transaction to see who receives the proceeds.

801,351,354 shares offered by Anthropic: the company receives the purchase proceeds and issues new stock.

23,648,646 shares offered by existing stockholders: the selling holders receive the proceeds; Anthropic receives none.

New issuance raises company capital; a secondary sale pays the selling holder. Resale eligibility alone is not a cash-flow measure.

Excludes the underwriter option and concurrent private placement. Offered shares are not a forecast of later sales, final price or money moving from Bitcoin. No proceeds are computed.

Share counts are reported preliminary terms. Millions rounded to two decimals; bar widths use exact 801,351,354/825,000,000 and 23,648,646/825,000,000 ratios. Flow arrows are schematic, not cash-amount scales. Both native options show reported transaction types.

Excludes the underwriter option and concurrent private placement. Offered shares are not a forecast of later sales, final price or money moving from Bitcoin. No proceeds are computed.

Under the preliminary IPO and concurrent private-placement assumptions, legal Class A and Class N shares together rise from about 11.9 billion to over 13 billion, an increase of approximately 9.66%.

The approximately 15.5 billion Class A-equivalent securities covered by lock-ups are another measure, including Class N shares, awards, and potential note conversions. The pool spans more securities than already-issued Class A stock and differs from freely tradable float.

Awards and convertible instruments can create additional shares when their conditions are met.

The preliminary resale disclosures allow up to approximately 316 million additional shares to become eligible for sale from the first trading day. Further quantities include 299 million at each of 27 and 48 days after the US prospectus date, and 349 million at each of 62 and 76 days.

Non-founder personnel and certain other holders have restrictions ending at the earlier first-quarter results trigger or 180-day endpoint. Co-founders and certain larger holders follow an earlier third-quarter results trigger or 365-day endpoint, with staged early-release exceptions.

Earnings-linked triggers use public results announcements and subsequent trading-day intervals, and representative waivers and other restrictions add further conditions.

Multiplying $1.5 trillion by 83% yields $1.245 trillion, but that's a theoretical value. That interpretation depends on what holders sell, the prices buyers pay, and demand for the stock

The Federal Reserve’s Nov. 13 H.8 release shows seasonally adjusted bank credit rising from $20.02 trillion on Oct. 28 to $20.08 trillion on Nov. 4, a $58 billion increase.

Published after Hayes’s essay, the release shows aggregate bank credit expanding over the later reported week. Future stress remains possible, and these totals provide no AI-specific lending breakdown or causal evidence about Bitcoin.

Hayes’s warning remains a scenario worth tracking: insider selling, weaker share prices, higher financing costs and reduced lending would support successive links in his argument.

Anthropic’s conditional IPO timetable brings the selling-risk test closer, while the transmission from share supply to Bitcoin liquidity still requires evidence.

#5012. CFTC backs blockchain-based derivatives infrastructure as Backpack, tZERO win approvals

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Monday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig said the agency had approved the applications, marking another sign of its increasingly crypto-friendly regulatory approach.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to establish regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that use blockchain technology to execute and settle transactions.

On Monday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig highlighted the approval of a blockchain-based derivatives exchange and clearinghouse, which appears to correspond to Backpack's newly announced U.S. regulatory approvals.

"These approvals mark an important milestone in the evolution of American financial markets and demonstrate that there is a regulated pathway for a new generation of market infrastructure built using blockchain technology," Selig said.

Financial tech company tZERO received its exchange approval last week, following its earlier approval from the agency to operate a derivatives clearing organization, which it says will allow the firm to "support derivatives trading and clearing through its own regulated entities."

"The approvals establish a unique new derivatives market infrastructure vertical within tZERO's growing Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) business, enabling the company to develop exchange and clearing services for financial institutions and other market participants," tZERO said.

Backpack announced its approval from the CFTC on Monday. In a statement, Backpack US President Mark Wetjen called the approvals a "really big deal."

"This is an achievement that demonstrates that the highest standards of regulatory compliance and blockchain innovation can go hand in hand," Wetjen said.

Over the past year, the CFTC under Selig has taken significant steps for crypto regulation, including working with the Securities and Exchange Commission to clarify which digital assets are securities or commodities, creating an innovation task force and supporting 24/7 trading and bitcoin perpetuals.

Selig, who currently serves as the CFTC's sole sitting commissioner, could soon have fellow commissioners. Last week, President Donald Trump tapped Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to be commissioners at the CFTC. The Senate Agriculture Committee will hold its nomination hearing for the bipartisan pair on Tuesday, after which their nominations could head to a full Senate confirmation vote.

#5010. Romesh Ranganathan, 48, Lost 44 Pounds by Keeping Fitness Simple—Here's How He Made Exercise Stick

The comedian says strength training, running and consistency—not vanity—have transformed his health.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Funny and self-deprecating on screen, Romesh Ranganathan takes his health and fitness seriously off it. He's not your typical gym-goer, though. Rather than training to build a bodybuilder's physique or hit performance milestones, his focus is on staying strong, healthy and active as he gets older—and being there for his three sons.

“I got a medical when I turned 40 as I started to worry about my own mortality, not for myself, but because of my kids,” he told On: Yorkshire Magazine. “Before, when I was going to the gym or staying on top of fitness, I'd do it for some sort of vanity reason. I've long since abandoned that and have accepted that I'm never going to look good. So the second half is about my reaction to that medical.”

Now 48, Ranganathan revealed on the Wolf & Owl podcast that he's been training more consistently in recent months. He has previously said he lifts weights three or four times a week—sometimes more if his schedule allows—while also trying to keep his daily step count high.

“I started hitting the gym for weights about three to four times a week, sometimes more if I fancied, and was trying to up my step count and cardio, but my appetite for that is a struggle,” he said in an interview with Huel.

It's an approach that has helped him lose around 44 pounds over the past few years.

Running has also become a key part of his fitness journey. After initially hating it, the comedian went on to complete the London Marathon in both 2024 and 2025.

The turning point came after one piece of simple advice.

“Running is something that people had always recommended to me. But as soon as I had a go at it, I found it unbearable. I'd go out for a run and be blowing after two minutes, then start walking, run a bit more, start blowing again. I'd come back and just feel absolutely battered,” he told Runner's World.

“Then somebody gave me the basic tip of just slowing down a little bit and getting on top of my breathing. That is the single most helpful tip I've ever had; suddenly I went from someone who couldn't face running to seeing all of the benefits of it. That's not to say that it suddenly became easy.”

Ryan is a Senior Writer at Men’s Health UK with a passion for storytelling, health and fitness. Having graduated from Cardiff University in 2020, and later obtaining his NCTJ qualification, Ryan started his career as a Trainee News Writer for sports titles Golf Monthly, Cycling Weekly and Rugby World before progressing to Staff Writer and subsequently Senior Writer with football magazine FourFourTwo.

During his two-and-a-half years there he wrote news stories for the website and features for the magazine, while he also interviewed names such as Les Ferdinand, Ally McCoist, Jamie Redknapp and Antonio Rudiger, among many others. His standout memory, though, came when getting the opportunity to speak to then-Plymouth Argyle manager Steven Schumacher as the club won League One in 2023.

Having grown up a keen footballer and playing for his boyhood side until the age of 16, Ryan got the opportunity to represent Northern Ireland national futsal team eight times, scoring three goals against England, Scotland and Gibraltar. Now past his peak, Ryan prefers to mix weightlifting with running – he achieved a marathon PB of 3:31:49 at Manchester in April 2025, but credits the heat for failing to get below the coveted 3:30 mark…

#5009. Situational Awareness Dumps Bitcoin Miners After Citadel Sale

Situational Awareness, the artificial intelligence hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, cut its bitcoin miner holdings sharply in the third quarter, leaving about $80.8 million across three stocks and exiting three others, a Monday filing shows.

The San Francisco firm still held 3,019,029 CleanSpark shares, worth $38.9 million at Sept. 30, 1,934,618 Bitdeer shares, worth $20.3 million, and 527,864 IREN shares, worth $21.6 million. Those are the only miner lines left, a sliver of the $1.83 billion in six miner stocks the fund listed at June 30.

The deepest cut was IREN. The fund held 9,474,099 IREN shares, worth $433.3 million, at midyear. The Sept. 30 stake is about 94% smaller by share count. CleanSpark was trimmed about 75%, from 12,276,139 shares worth $178.6 million. Bitdeer was reduced about 44%, from 3,439,450 shares worth $54.6 million. Bitdeer’s reported value fell further than its share count, to $20.3 million, as the stock also declined.

Three names disappeared from the filing entirely. The fund had held 26,008,473 Core Scientific shares, worth $665.6 million, 17,100,000 Riot Platforms shares, worth $468.2 million, and 9,133,726 Hive Digital shares, worth $33.2 million, at June 30. None of those lines appear in the new report. The filing does not say whether those sales were part of a late-July portfolio sale, later trades, or both.

Aschenbrenner published a long 2024 essay, “Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead,” arguing that artificial general intelligence was approaching faster than most investors appreciated, and that computing power and electricity would be the tight constraints. He founded the fund that September around that view, looking at technology and energy companies that AI would help or hurt.

The miner stakes fit the same idea. A March profile described the fund as betting that electricity and computing capacity may be the most valuable assets in the AI build-out, pointing to miners that were turning high-density facilities and power contracts toward AI workloads. IREN has signed a multiyear cloud contract with Microsoft. CleanSpark has struck a $6.6 billion data-center lease. Listed miners have also been operating under tight economics this year, with bitcoin often trading below estimated production costs.

The cuts landed after a brutal July. The fund sold the bulk of the fund’s public stock portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel late that month after heavy losses on AI-related holdings, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources said the fund was forced to unwind most of its public book. In a letter to investors, Aschenbrenner said the portfolio was down an estimated 67% in July, that the fund had come “closer to permanent capital impairment than is acceptable,” and that it had sold a portion of its public holdings in a block trade to remove all leverage and close its shorts. The unaudited letter still put year-to-date performance at plus 80%. Aschenbrenner said the fund was not shutting down and had preserved its private investments.

The new 13F shows how much of the public book was left by Sept. 30. Reported long holdings fell from $20.24 billion, across 26 lines, at June 30, to $1.58 billion, across 23 lines, three months later. That decline should not be read as the fund losing 92% of its capital. A 13F reports only long positions in U.S.-listed stocks and certain options. It leaves out cash, shorts and private investments, and option lines are valued at the underlying shares, not the premiums paid. Reuters’ sources said that after the Citadel deal the fund would hold a book of roughly $10 billion, including stocks and private investments such as a stake in Anthropic.

What remains is concentrated. The largest common-stock line is now SharonAI, 8,070,950 shares worth $440.7 million. Aschenbrenner also listed call options on Bloom Energy, SanDisk, Nebius and a memory ETF. The three leftover miner stakes are a stub of the midyear book. Whether those positions were trimmed further after Sept. 30 will only be clear when the fourth-quarter 13F arrives in mid-February.
